🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is +0.41% (intraday, 7-year -6bp). At trading day 27 (last close) it was +0.41% against a five-campaign average of -1.24% at the same point — 1994-95, 1999-00, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.84%. The 10-year is -3bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 2 of 4 signals: early signs of topping).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 803bp against a five-year average of 414bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +56bp and BB +42bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.61 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is moving too (+12bp in a month).
  • Bank Earnings: 9 banks reported (ABCB, ASB, COLB, EBC, FIBK, GBCI, WSFS, FHB, FLG); 3 red-flagged (ABCB: NPLs +17% QoQ; ASB: NPLs +22% QoQ; FHB: NPLs +16% QoQ). Credit deteriorating at the margin; deposit costs flat. Watch: ABCB, ASB, FHB.
  • Stocks: US stocks fell, the Dow dropped most, and fear rose slightly.
  • FX: Dollar edged up; euro and pound slipped; yen near 157, little changed.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq slipped below their 50-day average but stay above longer trend.
  • Sectors: Energy surged while consumer, telecom and staples stocks sold off today.
  • Credit/Spreads: Riskiest junk bonds are under heavy stress; it is spreading to better-rated bonds.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate: weakest borrowers and oil are the hot spots.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is slowly cooling, but oil is pushing volatile prices higher.
  • Tech Bubble: Tech valuations are far below 2000 mania levels, but credit looks complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Alphabet is the biggest reporter, Flex has the biggest expected move; IPO calendar empty.
  • Iran: We found no verified news for today; this year's war keeps oil risk high.
  • Warsh: Fed likely holds Wednesday; leaning hawkish, with a later hike possible.
  • Week Ahead: Fed decision Wednesday, PCE inflation data, and mega-cap tech earnings.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term, neutral medium term; oil and credit set the tone.
  • Trades: Own energy, hedge junk bonds, avoid long bonds, trim Nasdaq on bounces.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 2 sell, 20 hold long, 23 stay out
  • Regime Rules: S&P 500 risk-on; NDX risk-on, 4.1% above its sell trigger; trend intact; credit spreads widening
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.51 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 90th pctile, +31bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.

  • Bottom line: Oil shock plus spreading junk-bond stress means defense ahead of the Fed.

Friday was an energy-shock, risk-off close. WTI rose 3.82% to $103.27 and Brent 3.23% to $116.82, while US stocks fell broadly: S&P 500 -0.52% (-39.75) to 7623.68, Dow -1.23% (-652.82), Nasdaq -0.21%, Russell 2000 -0.29%. The VIX rose 0.42 to 19.45. The oil move fed straight into rates. The 2Y rose 4.22bp to 4.6818%, the 10Y rose 4.15bp to 4.9945% (just under 5%), and the 30Y hit 5.3221%. Gilts reached 5.356%. Versus the prior session, the selling was broad: 9 of 11 US sectors fell and only Energy (+2.51%), Info Tech (+0.35%) and Real Estate (+0.23%) gained. Europe (SX5E -0.31%, STOXX 600 -0.31%) and the Nikkei (-0.34%) also slipped. The biggest underlying story is credit. The Bloomberg HY contagion panel (as of 2026-10-22, descriptive, not a validated signal) puts the Caa-B gap at 786bp, versus a 5-year average of ~414bp and at the 100th percentile of its 5-year range. Caa OAS is 1111bp, +180bp in a month and +291bp in three months, the widest since 2020-04-16. The key question is whether the CCC stress is spreading. It is: single-B widened 65bp in a month to 325bp, Ba widened 51bp to 206bp, and IG widened 11bp to 87bp. The B-Ba gap is steady at 119bp (about its 5-year median), which means BB and B are being repriced together, not just CCC. The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen from 0.31 three months ago to 0.49 a month ago and 0.62 now, close to its 5-year median of 0.70, so the moves are becoming more synchronized. Headline index spreads still look benign (US IG OAS 0.87, 12th percentile; HY OAS 3.38, 26th percentile), so the damage is at the bottom of the quality ladder. Sentiment is defensive heading into FOMC week (Wednesday Oct 28) with a hawkish-leaning Fed under Chair Warsh.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

The one-month windows show a late-cycle, stagflation-tinged rotation. In the US, Energy leads (+11.07% 1m, +51.9% YTD), followed by defensives: Cons Staples +8.16%, Utilities +8.1%, Health Care +5.41%. Growth and cyclicals lag: Comm Services -9.12% 1m (-6.2% 1w), Info Tech -4.57%, Industrials -2.55%. Globally the pattern repeats: Energy +8.71% 1m, Staples +7.58%, Utilities +5.59%, Health Care +5.18%, against Comm Services -8.3%, Info Tech -6.27%, Industrials -4.05% and Materials -4.0%. Today broke the defensive pattern: Staples (-1.83%) and Utilities (-0.66%) sold off with cyclicals as yields rose, while Tech bounced (+0.35%). That suggests rates, more than growth fear, drove the session. On YTD performance, value/commodity (Energy) and quality growth (Info Tech +21.22% US, +26.03% global) still lead. Consumer Discretionary (-2.46% US, -7.62% global) and Comm Services are the laggards, consistent with an oil shock squeezing the consumer.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.51 vol points (14th percentile of the 50 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 103.3 (75th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 85bp (steeper by 8bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (117bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 22 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Moderately persistent, with diverging layers. The trend measures of core inflation are cooling slowly: median CPI, median PCE and trimmed-mean PCE are tagged 'falling' and the 16% trimmed-mean is flat, which the computed Core-Trend Sub-Score (rendered separately) reflects. However, headline pressure is rebuilding through energy. Flexible CPI is 6.1232% and rising (82nd percentile), and the Dallas distribution shows 28.9% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5-10%), against 25.8% falling. Breadth is therefore split rather than broad-based. Core PCE YoY at 3.00759% is still well above target, and 1-year breakevens (2.713%) above 5-year breakevens (2.4679%) show markets pricing a near-term oil-driven bump rather than an un-anchoring. The risk is that $100+ oil leaks from flexible prices into sticky ones (Core Sticky CPI 2.7765%, currently flat).

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000

8 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 57/100
Today looks far from the March-2000 dot-com peak on equity froth, and closest to it on credit and financial-conditions complacency. Computed Equity Froth readings are low: Nasdaq trailing P/E 41.04x is 16% of the way to the 175x peak, the stretch above the 200DMA is 8% of 2000 conditions (3.9% vs 50%), and semis P/E 37.21x is at 43%. Late-cycle catalysts are mixed. The 2s10s curve at 31.27bp registers 69%, while both PMIs show little rollover (9% and 10%). Tight credit stands out: IG spread at 127% and Baa-10Y at 151% of 2000-peak tightness. Macro regime: dollar 39%, commodities vs equities 200% (commodities are not cheap versus stocks, unlike 2000). Bear-market signposts are split. NFCI loose (154%) and VIX (154% on the complacency scale) flag easy conditions, while AAII (27%), consumer confidence (17%), put/call (48%), margin debt (40%) and SLOOS (58%) are well short of euphoria.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (41x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed panel describes an expensive but not manic market whose vulnerability is the credit cycle rather than speculative price excess. In 2000 the setup was extreme valuations, an inverted curve, cheap commodities and euphoric retail. Today valuations and price stretch are a fraction of that, sentiment is negative (AAII bull-bear -8.9pp), and commodities, especially oil, are expensive relative to stocks. The 2000-like features are elsewhere. Investment-grade and Baa spreads are tighter than at the 2000 peak and financial conditions are loose, even as the HY panel shows CCC spreads at 5-year extremes. That suggests a credit-led correction is more plausible than a 2000-style valuation collapse. The analyst-estimate inputs (top-10 S&P concentration ~39%, CAPE ~38x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth ~20/100, long-term EPS growth expectations ~65/100) are our rough judgement. They were not verified by web search in this run, so treat them as approximate and unsourced.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hold at the Oct 28 FOMC with a hawkish tone (analyst inference). One calendar preview (IFC Markets) expects a hold with a hawkish tilt and puts the policy rate at 3.75-4.00% after a September hike. That hike is NOT corroborated by our other sources and should be verified against the Fed. The 2Y at 4.6818% (+4.22bp today) is consistent with markets leaning hawkish.

~1 YEAR

Analyst inference: a hawkish-leaning path, with policy held at or modestly above current levels and a non-trivial chance of a further hike if $100+ oil passes through into core. At his first press conference (June 17, 2026), the Fed held at about 3.6% and nearly half of policymakers said they could back a hike later in 2026, a stance described as unexpectedly hawkish. Warsh said the committee was unanimous on price stability. Easing within a year likely requires core PCE (3.00759%) to fall clearly and the oil shock to fade.

Verified record from this run's searches: Warsh became chair after Powell's tenure ended in May 2026, held rates at his June debut, and stressed a unanimous commitment to price stability, alongside a dot-plot-style lean toward possible hikes (Sinclair-syndicated report, June 2026). We did not retrieve his earlier speeches or writings in this run. The view that he favors less forward guidance and a smaller balance sheet comes from his pre-chair public record as we recall it, not from a source cited here, so treat it as unverified inference. The IFC Markets claim of a September hike to 3.75-4.00% is a single unverified source and conflicts with no other evidence we found either way. The reaction function we infer: with core PCE at 3.00759%, flexible CPI at 6.1232% and rising, and 1y breakevens at 2.713%, a hawkish hold is the base case, and the press conference tone matters more than the decision.

Sources: All eyes on Kevin Warsh: New Fed Chair keeps rate unchanged, hosts first news briefing (KMPH/Sinclair) · IFC Markets — Market opportunities week 26-10-2026 to 30-10-2026
